section: Why use a stylesheet instead of styling each element?
text:
Why use a stylesheet instead of styling each element?
You can style an element inline with the style attribute:
<p style="color: red;">Red text</p>
That works for one element, but on a full website it gets long, repetitive, and error-prone. A stylesheet holds every rule in one place, and Quarto links it in the <head> for you when you list it in _quarto.yml:


_quarto.yml

format:
  html:
    theme: [cosmo, styles.scss]

title: Styling a Quarto Website with CSS/SCSS
section: How does CSS decide what to style?
text:
How does CSS decide what to style?
A CSS rule has two parts: a selector (what to style) and properties (how to style it).
h1 {            /* selector */
  color: teal;  /* property: value */
}

CSS selectors


Selector
Selects
Example




Tag
Every element of that type
h1


Class
Elements with that class
.demo-card


ID
The one element with that ID
#first-card


a, b
Both a and b
h1, h2


a b (space)
b anywhere inside a
p span


a > b
b exactly one level inside a
.demo-card > p


ab (no space)
Elements matching both
h2.title


*
Everything
.navbar *


:hover
Element under the mouse
a:hover


:active
Element being activated
.nav-link:active




Which rule wins when two rules target the same element?
That is the cascade in Cascading Style Sheets. The general rule: the more specific selector wins. A rule for h1.title (tag + class) beats a rule for h1 (tag only).

title: Styling a Quarto Website with CSS/SCSS
text:
What can CSS change?
CSS changes how elements look (colors, fonts, sizes) and how they are laid out. Every element follows the box model:

Content sits in the middle (light teal). Padding is the space between the content and the border. The border is the dashed coral line, set by color, style, and width. Margin is the space outside the border.

.box-demo {
  background: $theme-light-teal;   // content area
  padding: 1rem;                   // inside spacing
  border: 3px dashed $theme-coral; // color, style, width
  margin: 1.5rem 0;                // outside spacing
}
Padding and margin can be set all at once (padding: 1rem) or one side at a time (padding-top, padding-right, padding-bottom, padding-left). Sizes can be pixels, rem, or percentages of the parent element.

title: Styling a Quarto Website with CSS/SCSS
Styling a Quarto Website with CSS/SCSS
text:
What makes a design work?

Consistency: visitors notice what looks different and assume it matters. Styling everything from one stylesheet keeps attention on the right places.
A small palette: pick colors from brand guidelines or palette inspiration, save them as theme- variables, and make variations with lighten() and darken().
Few fonts: one for headings, one for body text, one for code. Familiar fonts are easier to read.
Accessibility: keep color contrast high, add alt text to images, make every link reachable by keyboard (Tab), and avoid blinking or flashing content. A contrast checker such as WebAIM’s confirms whether text passes.







Styling is trial and error



Open the browser’s developer tools (Inspect), find the element and its classes, test a rule like color: red to confirm the selector works, then switch to the real value.

title: Listings in Quarto
text:
A listing is an automatically generated list of content. You don’t build the list by hand. You tell Quarto where to look, and it reads the YAML front matter of each item (title, description, categories, image, date) to build the links.
A listing can go on any page: add a listing option to the page’s YAML header. The most familiar example is a blog’s landing page, but listings work just as well for projects, talks, or publications.

title: Listings in Quarto
section: Why use a listing on a portfolio?
text:
Why use a listing on a portfolio?

Large collections: no hand-written link for every item.
Growing collections: set it up once, then add a file whenever you have a new project.
Consistent presentation: every item uses the same template.

title: Listings in Quarto
text:
How do you start one?
The smallest possible listing uses all the defaults:
---
title: "Blog"
listing: default
---
With no options, Quarto lists every Quarto document in the same folder as the page, using each one’s title and description.

title: Listings in Quarto
text:
What options control a listing?

Listing options







Option
What it does
Used on this page




contents
Where to look: a folder, file, or YAML list
projects, links.yml


type
The template: default, grid, or table
grid, table


sort
Item order
"title"


fields
Which metadata to show
[title, description, categories]


field-display-names
Renames the column headers
Title → Project, Categories → Skills


sort-ui / filter-ui
Sort menu and search box
Turned off




The three built-in types

defaultgridtable


A blog-style list: one item per row with title, description, and an optional thumbnail.


Rectangular tiles laid out in a grid. Good for portfolios.


Literally a table of the items, with optional sorting and searching.

title: Listings in Quarto
section: Example 1: a folder of project pages (grid)
text:
Example 1: a folder of project pages (grid)
Each file in the projects/ folder is a full page on this site. Its YAML supplies the card content:


projects/cep-collins.qmd

---
title: "Collins College Enrollment & Retention"
description: "MSDM Culminating Experience Project, Group 3"
categories: [CEP, GA4, Digital Channels]
---

The listing points at the folder:


listings.qmd

listing:
  - id: project-pages
    contents: projects
    type: grid
    sort: "title"
    fields: [title, description, categories]

title: Listings in Quarto
section: Example 2: a YAML file of outside links (table)
text:
Example 2: a YAML file of outside links (table)
Some work lives somewhere else: a GitHub repo, a published deck, another website. Listing items don’t need their own pages. A YAML file can list them, using path for the URL, so clicking an item takes visitors off this site:


links.yml

- title: "GitHub profile"
  path: https://github.com/jakevns
  description: "Source code for my coursework and websites"
  categories: [Git, Quarto, R]

This table uses field-display-names to make it read like a portfolio: what the project is, what it involved, and which skills it shows. With only a few items, the sort menu and search box aren’t needed, so they’re turned off:


listings.qmd

  - id: project-links
    contents: links.yml
    type: table
    sort-ui: false
    filter-ui: false
    fields: [title, description, categories]
    field-display-names:
      title: "Project"
      categories: "Skills"

title: Listings in Quarto
section: How do you place more than one listing on a page?
text:
How do you place more than one listing on a page?
Give each listing an id in the YAML, then put an empty div with that id wherever it should appear. Text and other content can go before, between, or after listings:
::: {#project-pages}
:::

Some text between the two listings.

::: {#project-links}
:::
Beyond the built-in types, a listing can use a custom template that controls exactly how each item is laid out.

title: Listings in Quarto
section: How do you remove a listing page?
text:
How do you remove a listing page?
Removing a page works the same way as adding one: delete the files that generate it, then remove its entry from the navbar in _quarto.yml.

title: Dashboard
text:
How was it built?
The dashboard is a Quarto document with format: dashboard, written in R:

Layout: two pages (# headings), rows and columns (## and ### headings) with set heights and widths, a sidebar, and a tabset.
Cards: each chart is a code cell with a #| title: option.
Value boxes: ::: {.valuebox} divs with Bootstrap icons, filled with inline R values.
Theme: the cosmo Bootswatch theme plus a custom dashboard.scss, with chart colors matched to the theme.
Embedding: this page shows the dashboard in an <iframe>.
